entry.title: Georgia Tech’s Initiative to Strengthen Energy Security and National Defense

media:group.media:title: Georgia Tech’s Initiative to Strengthen Energy Security and National Defense
media:group.media:description: Georgia Tech’s Strategic Energy Institute and Georgia Tech Research Institute have funded an interdisciplinary initiative focused on the link between energy and national security. The program aims to identify vulnerabilities in energy infrastructure, defend against evolving cyber threats, and improve the resilience of critical U.S. systems, including those that support the military. It also seeks to build partnerships with government, industry, and national security stakeholders. SEI Executive Director Yuanzhi Tang said the investment was a strategic choice, reflecting Georgia Tech's role in anticipating emerging challenges.

entry.title: These Students Helped Seniors Stay Independent

media:group.media:title: These Students Helped Seniors Stay Independent
media:group.media:description:
How can better design help people stay independent as they age? In this video, Georgia Tech industrial design students partner with residents of A.G. Rhodes to create practical tools that make everyday activities easier, more accessible, and more empowering. By working directly with the people who use their designs, students develop solutions that support independence while helping older adults continue doing the things they love.
From adaptive gardening tools to a wheelchair-mounted flower vase that allows residents to transport their own arrangements, this collaboration demonstrates the power of human-centered design and real-world problem solving. The partnership between Georgia Tech and A.G. Rhodes shows how innovation, accessibility, and community collaboration can improve quality of life while giving students valuable hands-on experience designing for real people.
Read the full story here: https://news.research.gatech.edu/feature/essie-knows-best

entry.title: Nuclear Waste: What It Is — and What It Isn't

media:group.media:title: Nuclear Waste: What It Is — and What It Isn't
media:group.media:description:
Check out the full story here: https://research.gatech.edu/feature/nuclear-waste
When people hear “nuclear waste,” they often imagine glowing green sludge leaking into the ground — a scene straight out of science fiction. The truth is far less dramatic and far more manageable. In fact, all the civilian nuclear waste produced by U.S. power plants so far could fit on a single football field stacked just 10 yards high. Managed under strict safety protocols, this byproduct of nuclear energy poses manageable risk compared to the billions of tons of greenhouse gases from fossil fuels. Today, researchers at Georgia Tech and around the world are working on safer reactor designs, advanced monitoring, and innovative recycling methods to turn nuclear waste into new opportunities — from clean energy to ultra-long-lasting batteries and even power for space missions.

entry.title: Treating Uveitis with This Microneedle Innovation | Research for Real Life

media:group.media:title: Treating Uveitis with This Microneedle Innovation | Research for Real Life
media:group.media:description:
A breakthrough from Georgia Tech is changing how eye diseases are treated. This video explores how a microneedle developed through years of research allows doctors to deliver medication directly to the back of the eye—targeting inflammation at its source. For conditions like uveitis, where traditional treatments often fall short, this precision drug delivery approach offers a more effective way to reduce pain and protect vision.
Now being used in clinical care, the Georgia Tech microneedle technology is helping patients go longer between treatments while experiencing more consistent results. By reaching a part of the eye once considered difficult to access, this innovation is advancing the future of ophthalmology, vision restoration, and targeted therapy—demonstrating how research can lead to real-world impact for people facing vision loss.
Our mission is turning scientific discoveries into practical solutions people can use. From every corner of the state to the other side of the world, our research makes living better — for everyone.
More more information, read here: https://research.gatech.edu/real-life/microneedle?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social_post&utm_id=research_for_real_life&utm_content=research_for_real_life_microneedle

entry.title: This Tech Turns Tiny Movements Into Full Device Control

media:group.media:title: This Tech Turns Tiny Movements Into Full Device Control
media:group.media:description:
A slight head tilt or shoulder movement can mean independence. Developed at Georgia Tech, Kinemo is an assistive technology that uses physiological sensing to turn small, intentional movements into control of phones, tablets, and computers, helping people with limited mobility reconnect with their digital lives.
Created in collaboration with patients and clinicians at Shepherd Center and other partners, Kinemo has evolved from a research idea into a real-world solution that is intuitive, discreet, and personalized. By focusing on human-centered design, Georgia Tech researchers are transforming small movements into new possibilities for independence and quality of life.
🔗 Read the full story: https://research.gatech.edu/feature/kinemo

media:group.media:title: Georgia Tech Project ENGAGES
media:group.media:description:
For more information: https://projectengages.gatech.edu/
Project ENGAGES is a Georgia Tech STEM outreach program designed to enhance high school science education in Atlanta through partnerships with Coretta Scott King Young Women’s Leadership Academy, B.E.S.T. Academy, South Atlanta High School, Benjamin E. Mays High School, D.M. Therrell High School, Booker T. Washington High School, Charles R. Drew Charter School, and KIPP Atlanta Collegiate. This innovative program provides students with hands-on STEM learning experiences, real-world research projects, and direct mentorship from Georgia Tech scientists to build awareness of careers in engineering, science, and technology. Project ENGAGES also supports teacher professional development by immersing educators in active research labs, strengthening classroom instruction and curriculum. By expanding access to STEM education, fostering diversity in engineering, and preparing students for high-demand STEM careers, Project ENGAGES helps build a skilled workforce and drives the future of science and technology in the United States.
